whyChoose.title: What to Know Before You Talk to an Insurer

items.title: California's Clock Is Running
items.desc: You generally have two years from the crash date to file a personal injury claim in California, but that window shrinks dramatically if a government vehicle or road defect was involved. An attorney can help you figure out which deadline applies to your situation.

items.title: Comparative Fault Won't Automatically Sink Your Claim
items.desc: California follows a pure comparative fault rule, meaning you can still recover damages even if you're partly at fault for the crash, though your share of responsibility can reduce the amount. An independent attorney can help make sure the fault percentage assigned to you is fair.

items.title: Skip the Recorded Statement
items.desc: There's no cap on non-economic damages like pain and suffering under California law, but insurance adjusters often try to minimize claims early through recorded statements. It's usually best to let an attorney handle those conversations before you say anything on the record.

items.question: How long do I have to file a claim after a car accident in South El Monte?
items.answer: In most cases, California gives you two years from the date of the crash to file a personal injury lawsuit. If a government entity, like a city vehicle or a defect on a public road, was involved, that deadline can be as short as six months. It's worth talking to an attorney quickly so you don't lose your right to pursue a claim.

items.question: What should I do if my crash happened near Garvey Avenue or Rush Street?
items.answer: Try to document the scene with photos, get contact information from any witnesses, and seek medical attention even if injuries seem minor at first. These corridors see steady traffic, and public crash records show they're part of the higher-volume roads in South El Monte, so evidence can be easy to lose if it's not gathered quickly. An independent attorney can help you gather traffic camera footage or city records if needed.

items.question: Will I still get compensation if I was partly at fault for the accident?
items.answer: Possibly, yes. California uses a pure comparative fault system, which means you can still recover damages even if you share some responsibility for the crash, though the amount may be reduced by your percentage of fault. An attorney can help make sure your share of fault is calculated fairly based on the evidence.
